records.title: Show HN: Spotatui, a Spotify TUI/GUI without web API rate limits
records.author: LargeModGames
records.storyText:
About 11 months ago i revived the amazing but unfortunately unmaintained spotify-tui. Since then I have been working on it almost non stop, finding a lot of problems on the way.

One of the main issues I ran into were the Spotify web API rate limits. Third party clients like spotatui are dependent on a developer app made in the Spotify developer dashboard, which get rate limited a lot and Spotify has slowly been deprecating endpoints from it. The workaround for this used to be using a shared client id from ncspot but unfortunately that got rate limited too. This is when i started adding other playback sources, including YouTube, Navidrome/Subsonic, Internet radio with +- 30.000 stations, local files, Qobuz for lossless audio and Apple Music for macOS only where it controls the music app remotely.

I fixed both the deprecated endpoints and the rate limits with one solution. It still uses librespot in the back, my spotatui specific fork, but gets all data from it instead of only playback. The data comes from the internal API of the official clients, that API gives metadata, playlists, the user library, devices, lyrics and audio analysis. For searching it uses Pathfinder, the internal GraphQL API.

There are no web API rate limits because there is no shared app quota. Every user uses their own session as if it was the official client. The only potential problem is that Spotify does not document this API so any change on their side would break it. I intend to fix any of those issues as soon as they pop up.

It all started as a TUI back in 2019 but since then I've added a GUI to it too. The GUI is still a bit behind the TUI in terms of features, it only ships Spotify for now, but full parity between the TUI and GUI is coming soon. After that full parity with the official client is next. That is also why I made the GUI looks almost the same as the official client. That way its easier for me and users to find missing features.

Spotatui also has lua scripting support, a optional Web companion on spotatui.com, and if you have a AI coding agent like ChatGPT codex or Claude Code you can enable the MCP tools, which lets AI become your personal DJ just by talking to it.

Its written in Rust, uses ratatui for the terminal UI and Tauri 2 for the GUI. The Rust core starts a small web server with localhost that only your pc can reach which the GUI then serves. Both frontends share the same playback logic, the same login and the same Spotify code. The only difference is how you interact with it.

On first launch it opens a web browser where you need to login with your Spotify premium account (premium is not optional), that is the whole setup done. I would love any feedback about bugs you encounter or features you would like to see. GitHub: https://github.com/LargeModGames/spotatui Releases: https://github.com/LargeModGames/spotatui/releases/latest Website: https://spotatui.com/

Thanks to librespot for making this all possible

records.title: Show HN: Chkit – Schema, migrations and backfills for ClickHouse (like Drizzle)
records.author: keks0r
records.storyText:
Hey HN, im Marc, co-founder of ObsessionDB. We are open sourcing ChKit, our tooling to manage schemas, migrations and backfills for clickhouse.

I am a big fan of the type safety drizzle provides for the database. Manage the schema in typescript and generate migrations from it is a powerful workflow. I always wished something like it would exist for clickhouse, so we could manage our analytical workloads the same way. It didn't exist, so we build it.

We build it after running ClickHouse at petabyte scale in our previous company, were we managed hundreds of tables, MVs and endpoints reading from them.

The way it works:

1. You define your schema in typescript, with typed helpers for tables, mv, column types etc.. 2. You generate the migration, that contains the DDL, to get your clickhouse instance from status quo to what your current typescript schema defines 3. Your CI can check for drift 4. You run the generated migration against production 5. You use the defined types in your code, to ingest your data while making sure it has the correct type. Bonus: if your schema change was BC breaking, we generate the sequence on how to backfill the data, into the intermediate table to migrate (this is quite the hard problem with large tables and schema evolution)

In case you have already a clickhouse instance with a schema, you can pull it down and start using ChKit from where you are.

Run our generator to setup the boilerplate:

  npm create chkit@latest
If you folks are running clickhouse in production, I am curious to hear what other challenges you are running into.

records.title: Show HN: Stream live open data in two commands
records.author: gardensalad
records.storyText:
A service and open source tool to get open data streams in two commands. No sign up needed for subscribing.

Streams to try:

- https://hypermass.io/stream/_J0fm450s - extreme UV images of the sun from SOHO - visual data

- https://hypermass.io/stream/_ATtCoEK - GDACS live disaster data (filtered to just the ongoing items)

The CLI (Apache 2.0, https://github.com/hypermass-io/hypermass-cli) tool allows you to subscribe to multiple live streams of files, with the files arriving in a local folder. The filenames are ULIDs so they can be easily sorted into time order in scripts and code. Publishing works similarly - drop files into a folder and they get read, published and deleted locally. The idea is that by being highly opinionated about the shape of the data (files, delivered in sequence, in real time) a bunch of the logic and edge cases get handled well in one place (things like ordering, retries, hash verification, reconnection, etc) - rather than requiring every subscriber to implement it themselves for every source.

A high-speed version for things like departure boards, train positions is in the pipeline.

Background: About 10 years ago, I worked for a few years supporting and developing some of the UK Rail Open Data systems. As a developer I was frustrated at how fragmented the open data space was, and how every open data system was designed as a blank-page exercise. I realised that a lot of data falls into an odd middle ground, too infrequent to economically poll on a large scale, too large for messaging protocols, but in some sense still real time. For example transport schedules, periodic solar imagery, disaster alerts - real-time but infrequent.

Fairly often I just wanted a "just give me the data" option when the solutions I found were static catalogues with no nod towards real-time use, bespoke APIs, analytics systems and other things I didn't need. I couldn't find a simple approach that leaned into what I saw as the data's strengths (simple files, delivered in order, as/when they are published) - so I built it.

About me: Solo founder based in the UK, full time for just over a year.

Sustainability: Initially a "heavy users pay for more data allowance" model with a decent free tier. Ideally we later shift to institutional publishers pay to keep their streams free to download. Possibly a paid data marketplace to support costs, but the main focus would always be the free and open data.

What I'd like to know:

- Does the CLI approach solve any real problems for you?

- Is the technical approach sane?

- Would you use a service like this to publish data?

- Recommendations to bootstrap users (particularly publishers)?

records.title: Show HN: shadowclone, skills learned from your coding agent corrections
records.author: theonly1me
records.storyText:
shadowclone reads the coding-agent sessions already on your disk, finds where you corrected the agent and turns those corrections into skills your agents load next time. It supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi, and Antigravity. Every capture source is off by default and has its own consent setting.

Why I'm building it?

I use multiple harnesses and agents, I extensively use Claud Code and Codex, but I also use Cursor and Antigravity every now and then. I didn't want to have to teach every harness or model the things I taught the other ones between my last session and the current one. I also cannot have my personal rules and preferences in all the repositories I work on because my collaborators may have varying levels of trust with AI and their own preferences. shadowclone helps me build and improve trust with my agents so I can give them more autonomy while running multiple sessions in parallel.

---

Who is this for?

If you only use Claude or Codex or any one of these, you may not need the shadowclone CLI and the harness and agent you use might already be sufficient. But, if you are like me and work across harnesses and agents, shadowclone will help you avoid repeating your preferences each time.

---

Built-in skills and skill builds

shadowclone is also great for someone who is just now adopting AI into their coding workflows because it ships with several skills that they can use to customize their agent's behavior. They can equip all the skills, or just some of them, they'll see the "personality" their agent gets from equipping those skills from the `shadowclone wizard`.

---

Setup is extremely easy, just ask your Claude Code, or Codex, or another agent -

"Set up shadowclone: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/theonly1me/shadowclone/mai..."

---

Privacy

shadowclone is free and open source, it uses the MIT license. It doesn't have a subscription, or a server. It just uses your existing agent subscription i.e. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, or even your local model via Pi. You can explicitly disable sources, it also redacts any and all sensitive information it uses for learning.

---

PR reviews and Cloud bots

It can review PRs with the `shadowclone review` command, it ships a guided review skill that will perform a deep review of your code (or someone else's) and produce an HTML document you can annotate, add comments to and submit so your agent can stage a draft review on the PR you are reviewing.

records.title: Show HN: Laya guard – a local check before your coding agent runs a command
records.author: ayaan0209
records.storyText:
HN, this is my first Show HN post, and I'm really nervous, I'm Ayaan, a Frontend Developer.

laya-guard is a local check that occurs before any coding agent tool call, deciding whether to approve, send for review, or block the call.

When Jev was released, I was curious as to how I could use it, and I quickly discovered Laya which is an open-source 322M model that functions almost identically but runs on a laptop's CPU in under 100ms, as the check is local, there won't be a chance of 3rd parties seeing your commands, directories, or tokens, and there's no charge per call, I often work in Korean, and most of the guardrails I've seen have not evaluated Korean at all, hence why I've implemented it as well.

Regex policies catch known dangerous patterns before even reaching models, any command that is blocked is never seen by models, commands like ls, git status, and npm test will skip the model altogether, unless they have pipes, chaining, redirects, -exec flags, or sensitive paths, everything else is sent to the model for processing, once you have the model downloaded, it makes decisions from a fixed set of outcomes with no API key or request needed for any external service, there are also hooks for 11 different agents including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and many more.

And Also a local dashboard where you can see all decision and why it was made and install the hook for each agent, it doesn't save the commands themeslves.

In my tests with AgentDojo, it blocked 25/27 attacks, and allowed 92/97 harmless tasks, it correctly identified 64/66 commands I made.

After the Reddit post, people have found some issues with it:

Adding a comment at the end of a command would fool the model to not block the command.

The model only read the first 4,000 characters, so it could be spammed with junk to the beginning to bypass the check, this would send dangerous commands like curl to review.

"curl" repeated 40,000 times caused one regex to run for 48 seconds, timing out the hook and running the command.

All 3 issues have already been fixed, somebody also pointed out that if the server was down, commands ran without any check, now it asks you first, or blocks the command if the agent can't ask

Please note that this is not a tool to check if the code written is correct, it's a tool to prevent agents from running dangerous commands.

records.title: Show HN: Ret – An inbox and canvas for your Codex and Claude Code agents
records.author: itsjustmechris
records.storyText:
Over the last few weeks I've really been using Codex and Claude to solve a lot of parallel tasks, across a lot of different projects. This lead me to wishing that I could interface with my agents in the same way that I interface with my already existing windows and editors. For me, this usually means that I have like 5 to anywhere around 8 different windows that I drag around depending on where I want to focus, this could mean I am focusing on the terminal now, or I want to test stuff in a simulator or browser; but when I go to interface with agents, I have to manage many tabs, or I have to look through a list in their native apps. This is not convenient for me, and I'm almost certain this is not convenient for many of you.

That's why I built an infinite canvas, where my traditional desktop style workflow can come to life alongside my agents, I can drag them around depending on where I want my focus to be, or I can let them just pile up, like the 15 finder windows you're hiding with your browser right now. But, when I do want to go back to that thread, I will intuitively just know right where it is.

I didn't stop there though, I really enjoyed the inbox style agent interface that Google shipped many months ago with Anti Gravity, but I didn't really enjoy much other than that, so, I built that in too.

But, I still didn't stop there, a traditional code editor still comes in handy every once and awhile, just to read, or to tradcode, though Ret doesn't feature a VS-Code fork, yet anyways, maybe one day something similar could exist, it does feature a fairly comparable implementation, powered by the same technology, in a similar layout, just without the plugins and bloat.

But, I didn't stop there either, the traditional sidebar and one centered chat is a nice experience sometimes, so I built that in too.

I guess you probably can see where this is going, but that's also not where I stopped. Working on a single focused thread can be beneficial, but I am a heavy fork user, so I made it convenient to work side by side your main thread and a fork, with ambitions to expand on this in the future as I feel out how many forks or side chats are worth working on at the same time in the 'focused' view. But focus view doesn't stop there, instead of having only one chat in focus, and having to then jump back to the sidebar, I thought, well hey, browser tabs are great, so I built those in too.

I know it sounds like there's a lot of things built in here, and there is, but trust me, it doesn't feel bloated at all, it feels amazing. I really think this is something that greatly benefits my productivity, and I hope that some of you also feel my excitement when trying it out.

records.title: Show HN: Helicon – Desktop App for Meta's Muse Code CLI (Linux, Windows, macOS)
records.author: harjjotsinghh
records.storyText:
Hi Hacker News, I'm Harjot. I've been using Meta's Muse Code CLI daily for a few weeks now. One thing that I found difficult to handle was managing or controlling multiple sessions across multiple projects, while using the terminal for the muse CLI. Initially, I used cmux to create workspaces/groups for my different projects to group them, and then created 4 split terminals in each of those projects, that ran muse code sessions in each of them. It worked, but it was ugly. I didn't like using that. It could be because I'm not really a terminal person and would much rather prefer a proper dedicated GUI or desktop/app interface, and I would prefer it any time over a terminal screen or CLI. So it might be personal preference but yeah.

So, I started building a desktop app around it, mainly to scratch my own itch.

Helicon is a desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux, plus a VS Code extension that also works in Cursor and Devin. It doesn't replace the CLI. It runs `muse serve` and talks to it, and it reuses your existing `muse login`, so you don't have to get an API key and you don't pay an extra bill. You can use your existing Muse Code subscription plans.

Some things that I use the most: 1. Resuming sessions that I started in the terminal. I don't start many sessions in the terminal now that Helicon exists, but initially I wanted to access all the sessions that were running in a terminal to be accessible from Helicon, when it was created initially. 2. Inline diffs that I can approve, similar to how Cursor works. 3. I can clearly see my 5-hour and weekly plan limits directly from the app itself and don't have to manually keep going to Meta's Muse Code billing page and manually keep refreshing the page to see my current usage/limits.

I built it using Tauri 2 and React. It is MIT licensed. I built a lot of it with AI coding agents, especially Opus 5.5 (I really like using this model). It's at v0.21.9 now, and 9 people have contributed so far.

Some issues: the Windows installer isn't code-signed yet, so you'll see a SmartScreen warning. And the macOS build isn't notarized, so you need to click "Open Anyway" once.

You can try it in the browser with mock data, no install needed: https://helicon.sh/try

It's unofficial and not affiliated with Meta.

If you use a coding CLI every day, what would you want from a GUI for it? And what would make you go back to the terminal?

records.title: Show HN: 4B VLM trained on 600k questions to query images in one pass
records.author: aditmag
records.storyText:
Heyo!

I'm Adit, an undergrad in Finland. This is a preview of a side project I worked on last weekend. Essentially, Dragonfly is a LoRA fine-tune of Qwen3-VL with typed output heads that answers many questions about an image in one pass, with a probability for every answer. Unlike a VLM that generates an answer to each question, Dragonfly reads the image once and scores every question in the same pass. Questions can't see each other, so each answer is the same as asking it alone, in any order.

Instead of text outputs, Dragonfly answers with calibrated probabilities for the options you give it in order to answer the question. You can ask Dragonfly multiple choice, yes/no, or scale-based questions.

As you might have guessed already, I got the idea from Jev and thought it would be fun to train a small model that can do the same thing for images. There wasn't a dataset for questions specifically, so I compiled a couple open datasets to form around half of our training data and then distilled Qwen to generate ~300k questions that I could verify against the human annotated data.

Try it out @ https://adit.run/dragonfly and lmk what you think :)

records.title: Show HN: Lightweight, self-hosted, web analytics app
records.author: composer42
records.storyText:
Hey everyone! I just wanted to share a little project I have been working on. It's a lightweight, minimal, self-hosted, web analytics app alternative to Google Analytics, Umami, GoatCounter etc.

Tldr: Created a self hosted web analytics app that is one binary (docker image available). AI was used to assist. Check it out if you care.

I wanted to self host a lightweight web analytics app to see if any of my pages had any visitors, but all of the self hosted apps I found were either way to heavy for what I was looking for, or simply didn’t have a UI/UX I liked. So I just made one myself.

The app features a dashboard with multi-site and subdomain support, and some simple filtering on date and visitor details (all EU regulation friendly, so no PIs such as IPs etc).

A bit about the process:

As I wanted it simple and lightweight, a single executable was the goal. Deciding for the frontend was easy since it doesn’t need SEO or any server side rendering, therefore I chose React with plain CSR (thankfully the DX these days is nice with Vite). The backend was a bit more tricky, since I wanted to have it fast, but also be able to get an MVP out sooner rather than later. The plan was thus two folded; first to do it in Deno to keep everything TypeScript and to implement features fast (it is still my go-to language for prototypes), then to refactor everything to a compiled language (Go or Rust) once I considered the app feature complete.

So I started the prototype, but just a couple of days later, the announcement of Deno being sunset came out. As I had already gotten to a point where the backend was mostly functional, I decided to pull the plug early and refactor! The tough decision was Rust vs Go, and Rust ultimately won as I like the DX and how the language looks and writes a wee bit more. So I did what most engineers do in 2026 (looking at you Bun), and I asked my AI for help. Although I consider myself pretty ok with Rust, there are still parts that I haven’t wrapped my head around fully, so as the intention was to get something out fast, I had to bite the bullet. Lastly for the database I wanted something embedded, so SQLite was the natural choice.

The final app ended up with a decent ~10mb (down from ~250mb with Deno) which I don’t think is too shabby. Some quick benchmarking on 1 cpu and 2gb RAM told me it could handle ~16.000 incoming analytics requests per second. The bottleneck being the database writer lock (give it more CPU, and it can do better). As this is a hobby project, and I dont expect a peak load of more than maybe 10 a day, I am content with this.

I consider this app mostly feature complete, and will use it for the next month before eventually releasing a v1 after fixing whatever bugs that may show themselves. If you think you can improve the app further and want to spend time on it, feel free to make a PR ^^

To sum up the stack: React+Vite+TanStack+Tailwind frontend, Rust+Axum backend and SQLite database; all compiled to one binary of about ~10mb.

Disclaimer: Yes, AI has been used for parts of the development, docs and for commit messages, but the code has been reviewed and iterated over by me, a somewhat reasonably sentient human.

records.title: Show HN: Search for AI agents with usefulness score built in
records.author: Ayobamiu
records.storyText:
Hi HN. I partnered with Simon Kley to build this project at innovation intelligence hackathon (Berkeley).

Simply, we’re building a usefulness score on top of search for ai-agents.

Instead of agents reading 10 ranked relevant pages, we run a usefulness score first and give it only those that pass. We’re able to save token and cost with this and slightly better answers.

During our research, we found out that the current search results already do justice when it comes to simple queries. The rankings work well. They struggle when the task requires deep research or recency matters. So, we decided to talk to devs building ai-agents that research companies for sales outreach. Deep research and recency matters a lot to them. And in their words “every so often, stale facts reach emails.” They catch them by someone responding to the email or human review.

From our tests, When an agent got outdated alert for 7 companies, it pitched outdated news for 4 out of them.

Talking to the engineers already building this agents, we learned that cost saving is not the real goal. They’re ready to pay premium for confident results. So we added another check to our score. We call it superseding score, it check for pages replaced by newer news. For example, if two recent pages were fetched for news on Humane ai pin. If the first talks about how groundbreaking the product is and the second did that + talked about the HP acquisition, then the second page supersedes the first. The first page gets a lower score.

We’re looking for feedbacks here and also teams that are building agents that research companies for outreach. Thanks.

Plus, we rank a page once and every agent reuses it, so the more the agents use us, the cheaper the search gets.

records.title: Show HN: Enso Method – agent skills for building software for someone else
records.author: dwkerwin
records.storyText:
The Enso Method is a new set of AI skills for Claude Code and Codex which I've open sourced on GitHub predominantly for developers who build for someone else who is making the product/business calls.

I've been using AI to write basically 100% of my code since late 2024, back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, when it barely worked and there were few people doing this and very little support for this way of developing. I stubbornly thought this was going to be the future and came up with a methodology for making it work, before "AI skills" were even a thing. Since then I've continued to refine the method and I just recently published it as open source. The method focuses on requirements (PRD, TDD) up front, and has skills that autonomously refine the requirements, declaring assumptions that should be validated by stakeholders. It doesn't expect you to be a solo founder or that whoever is at the keyboard directing Claude or Codex to be the product owner and business decider in addition to being the developer. I think most of us sit in the seat where we develop for someone else who decides. And if AI is all about velocity, then if we have to slow down to get product owners to review and decide, that puts a serious damper on the efficiency everyone expects from AI development. So a defining attribute of the Enso Method is, when it reviews the requirements prior to implementation, it asks what questions/gaps there are and it tries to answer its own questions. If it can get to 95%+ confidence in the answers, it just rolls with those. If less then it will declare the assumption in an assumptions.md file which gets routed to business stakeholders to review. In the meantime however we still consider this to be a green light, we can move forward and implement with the assumptions, and if we later hear from the business that the assumption was wrong, we update the requirements and re-implement, because implementation is now cheap, and waiting isn't.

records.author: iushh
records.storyText:
I made a text/language identifier today, in a single C file, with no ML.

It classifies a text by checking which reference text a hand-rolled greedy LZ77 compressor finds least surprising. Each class is just a file of reference data. For a query, it sums the bits the compressed output would cost against each reference, and the cheapest one wins. It never writes a compressed file.

I got this idea after watching 3b1b's compression is intelligence series for the 3rd time, so i had to make sure i understand it finally.

I have my intro to C exam tomorrow, so feedback on the C is welcome.

records.title: Show HN: Hapsland – Realtime semantic advice on coding standards for the agents
records.author: Firfi
records.storyText:
Agents ignore AGENTS.md mid-session.

Then you tell them: hey, this is written in AGENTS.md.

- "You're absolutely right!" (proceeds with fixing)

But not anymore! This is a tool that would check the code immediately with a classifier (Jev etc.) and give the agent advice in the same turn.

It catches some mistakes that are difficult to put into lint rules and excels at the cases when semantic understanding is required - e.g. field names/types in a nested structure that contradict each other (more commonly known as "invalid states") (that we strive to make, e.g. "unrepresentable", some would say)

Even reviewer agent loops won't do much (as Primeagen's X post a month ago shows in all the colours [which I don't know if I can or can not link, and will stay on the safe side of not doing so]). This may or may not have an influence in nerd sniping me into writing that tool.

In cases like these, Hapsland (or its approach, at least) comes to help.

I know, I know, Abide (look it up!) exists, but I wanted (a) semantic expansion of code (b) full control over what's sent to Jev (hey, their ToS aren't that privacy-friendly) (c) less footprint on the file system. So I made it compatible. In case you want to use both, I mean.

TLDR: catch a change with a coding agent hook => expand it into semantic code structure, respecting privacy settings => call Jev with your own code semantic rules => deliver feedback to the agent in the same turn, in 0.5s.

I also got a recording feature, there I had a big problem with the piano accompaniment coming through the speaker and tried to subtract it from the recording, but it still doesn’t work too well sadly. Lately I rewrote my page turn logic to do half page turns, cause every musician knows how frustrating it is to not see the next notes until the page turns.

My big vision is a bit unrealistic, but I want to somehow host all public domain pieces there are for free for all instruments, so people don’t have to pay $20 anymore for some Danse macabre euphonium arrangement for example... records.storyText:
Hi HN, I built Rollport, a cross-platform app (Windows, Mac and Linux) to import photos/videos from my iPhone to my computer, because the Windows Photos app always crashed and I do not want to use iCloud Photos or similar services. I just wanted a simple solution.

records.title: Show HN: Forkcast, a meal planner and tracker with focus on weekly planning
records.author: tizzyapunkt
records.storyText:
Hej HN, I’m Tizzy. I built forkcast, a meal planner and calorie tracker that is built around planning the week ahead instead of ad hoc tracking

Demo (runs fully in your browser, no sign-up): https://check-forkcast.tizzy.dev/demo/ Repo: https://github.com/tizzyapunkt/forkcast

After signing up for a 90-day challenge to lose weight and get fitter, meal planning and meal prepping have been the most important things, next to exercising oc. The apps that have been suggested for planning and tracking (yazio, fddb, MyFitnessPal), were nice for logging what I just ate but annoying to use as a planning tool so this is where forkcast comes from and how it works differently:

- You plan the week against your calorie and macro goals and see which days goals are met. Recipes are logged as their ingredients, not as one entity, which makes swapping ingredients or changing amounts a lot easier eg changing 100g of pasta for 75g of rice.

- Recipes serve two purposes. Logging them (leaving out ingredients that do not make sense to log, like herbs) and cooking them (seeing steps and all ingredients).

- The grocery list comes straight out of the weekly plan (and can go to Bring! if supported where you live). Packaged food comes from Open Food Facts, generic food from a local, editable catalog which is seeded with common foods.

- AI only where it saved me time which was importing recipes from photos and reading nutrition labels. It’s optional and uses your own Anthropic key.

Full disclosure at this point: I decided to build something that works for me, a dad of two (when I started they were two under two), full-time job, but still ready to get in shape! I would have loved to code this myself, since I am a software engineer and techie by heart, but my time was limited to reading specs, reviewing code and steering Claude Code. Without that, I would not have anything usable.

The stack is Hono + React PWA and deliberately kept without a real DB, multi-user or the like. Self-hosting is possible with docker and under AGPL.

I am posting to find out if anyone besides me finds this useful, and if so, whether a hosted version would be worth building besides the self-hosting option. There is a one click vote on https://check-forkcast.tizzy.dev Any feedback is welcome, even if it's just 'wow, yet another calorie tracker'.

Oh, and in the meantime, I found out that the clever and creative name I thought I came up with was chosen several times already. Meh. Ideas welcome. :)

records.title: Show HN: Pulse Local, a Mac budgeting app whose AI models run on your machine
records.author: niztk
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Niz. Pulse Local is a budgeting app for Mac (Apple Silicon, beta) that answers questions about your spending with models that run on your machine. Local mode needs no account. The ledger and your questions stay on the machine, and the app sends no analytics or crash logs.

How it works: you import a CSV from any bank, in any currency. When you ask a question, a tuned Qwen3 0.6B model reads it into a structured query, and code, not the model, does the money math against the ledger. A 4B checker model double-checks each money answer; when the two readings disagree, the app says it is not sure instead of guessing. That change took wrong answers from about one in five to 5 in 494 questions across our last three tests. The write-up covers how we test, the designs that failed, and the limits of the claim: https://pulseos.finance/pulse-local/writing/agree-or-not-sur...

The tuned weights are on Hugging Face (PulseOS/pulse-local-qwen3-0.6b).

Limitations: the first start downloads about 2.9 GB of models. With the checker on, a money answer takes 12 to 14 seconds (you can turn the checker off). Small models can still misread an open-ended question. The app answers in English. Mac only for now; Windows is next.

The app is free. An optional Connected mode (Sync Pass, $29/year) syncs US banks through Plaid; transactions pass through our server's memory and are not stored.

Feedback welcome, especially on wrong answers and on questions it should handle but does not.

records.title: Show HN: Proofsource. Find where AI leaves you out. And Fix it
records.author: lcbasu
records.storyText:
Hi HN. I am Lokesh.

I built Proofsource as an internal tool to help my finance ERP product , Rivane, to gain visibility into AI engines like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Google AI mode and such. But when I talked about it to my friends, they also saw value in it and it became a product of itself. And now proofsource had 5 paying customers(paying $1500pm in total) in the first week itself and more than 60 brands used it to get their visibility since we launched out of beta last week.

What proofsource does is that it queries ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude and Google AI Overviews using the questions or prompts that buyers normally ask and then it shows then which competitor shows up instead of their own brand for the questions/prompt. It also gives visibility into which sources the answers cite and other things like sentiments. Everything is shown to you along with what to fix and how each data and number is calculated to give 100% transparency into what we did and why and how you can use all this information to improve your visibility.

We are still adding features based on initial user's feedback like auto fixing and publishing to their social and web platforms. Running ads for them for improving the visibility.

We are just learning as we interact with each customer so feel free to share your feedback.

And thank you for your time. :)

records.title: Show HN: Indigene – native plants for where you stand
records.author: olivierlacan
records.storyText:
Back when I lived in Central Florida, it took me years to learn what native plants could benefit wildlife and the local ecosystem as I slowly replaced parts of my yard to make it more resilient to drought. After moving to Seattle a few years ago, I had to start all of that from scratch. LLMs made the process a bit easier but I still had to routinely ask the same kinds of questions over and over, despite being far more familiar with native plants these days and leaning more on native plant societies and botany resources like Doug Tallamy and Joey Santore whose excellent Crime Pays But Botany Doesn't site was recently posted here[1].

A good friend was visiting from Orlando over the summer and told me she was struggling to decide what to plant in her own yard despite her landlord being ok with it. That was enough of an excuse for me to kick off work on Indigene, which is aimed at giving folks just-in-time knowledge about what to plant based on their locale, sun exposure, soil conditions, and their own ecosystem support goals.

Candidly, as many of us have, I've also leaned heavily on LLMs (mostly Claude here) to bring this to life. Largely to avoid saying demonstrably false things, which might be an absurd statement. You can find the GitHub repository[2] a wild array of open data sources I've dug out and cross-referenced to ensure mistakes and hallucinations are unlikely to survive for long. But given today's Indigenous Peoples Day I figured it was past time I shared the projects and invited more scrutiny.

Being the Keep a Changelog guy, you can bet it has extensive release notes[3] generated from the project changelog. Those are also parsed into feature-specific guides so each also lists relevant recent updates.

Lastly, I put together a post[5] that goes into a bit more detail on the story of the project and what I've learned along the way.

I really, really hope people here (and beyond) find it as useful and enlightening as I do.

PS: before it comes up, all the LLM usage for the project is documented[6] and used as warning system in every PR but I think there's a lot more I can do to further reduce it

I recently had an issue with my right hand, and couldn't use it very effectively. So I was trying to figure out how I could still get work done without typing everything with my right hand.

records.title: Show HN: Ever – A High-Level Language for Low-Level Purposes
records.author: pouya1dev
records.storyText:
Hi everyone. Today I’m here to introduce "Ever". a language aiming to be something like a modern-day Turbo C. It features high-level syntax but operates at a low level, designed to run on modern systems.

By the way, don't download the release. That release is from three months ago—back when I created the previous thread—and work on the new version isn't finished yet, so I haven't released it. I started this thread to get your opinions and feedback on the new version.

I can no longer say that the entire language is written in D, because I’ve written the libraries and the Windows interpreter in various languages. However, I can still say that the core of the project is largely written in D.

Ever is made possible thanks to the D community. arsd.simpledisplay and arsd.minigui provides high-level graphics functions, making it easy to create graphical applications. I'm also working on integrating Raylib with Ever to make game development possible.

And to test and build the language, simply run the following command. curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/evrlang/ever/main/install.... | bash

Or clone the repo and run compile.sh.

I sincerely apologize that the documentation isn't finished yet and I haven't had time to add more examples. However, if you have any questions, feel free to reach out to me here so I can help you.

Github link: https://github.com/evrlang/ever Website: https://evrlang.github.io/ever A very special thank you to everyone who gave me technical advice on the previous thread and prompted me to reconsider the language syntax.

records.title: Show HN: Henge Days – When does sunlight directly hit the wall of a building?
records.author: busseio
records.storyText:
I've been a photographer for decades, and for a long time I've wanted to make an app that will tell me when the sun's light will directly hit the/a surface of a building.

This weekend I found the time to build and launch a thing that does that. Features include:

  - Enter an address, get back a map with calendar details and some dataviz on when the sun is going to hit each wall

  - Save buildings, walls, and dates in a Planner, with a Calendar feed

  - Analyze the sun between two points along a street (currently limited to 5km along a single street)

  - Share links to what you've found
Sources used include: OpenStreetMap, Nominatim, Photon and the US Census Bureau geocoder. Sun positions come from the NOAA solar position algorithm, computed in-browser. Cloud forecasts from Open-Meteo.

I hope you find it useful, and welcome feedback!

records.title: Show HN: Authrot – extract your story elements out of chapters and graph them
records.author: JoeOfTexas
records.storyText:
I've been working on this app for a couple months, because I needed help outlining my story being written on Google Docs.

I kept adding new characters, and it was difficult for me to keep track of everything going on in the story. I wasn't organized at all.

I do have a subscription to Claude, and it helps, sure, but it didn't exactly build a graph of all the story elements connecting together. Throwing 20 chapters into one context was just terrible at narrowing its focus.

I started building this tool as a way to help me with a few things...

First, was replace Google Docs, because that thing lagged like crazy after 20~ chapters.

Second, was scanning my chapters. I wanted to automate creating a graph of characters, places, factions, objects, monsters, everything. I even started mapping out plots, threads, promises, and events. I threw it all into a database, and am able to lay it all out on the table, in an easy to absorb format.

Want to see where someone traveled throughout the story? What about when they encountered others? Well, now I can! Replacing names and all their aliases throughout the whole book? Easy peasy. What about fixing plot holes? No problem, we can fix those too.

Anyways, I took the extra effort to make it available for everyone by throwing it on on k3s and building the extra framework around the workspace.

It's completely free to use. Scanning chapters requires AI credits, which you get 50 for free at signup. Enough to scan about 15 chapters, or start a new story.

If you need more credits, let me know and I'll gift you more.
